"You've won the National Merit Cash Award, fifty thousand rupees," the caller said. "Only a 1,500 processing fee to release it today."
Hrithik was standing in the corridor outside the college accounts office, which almost felt like a sign. He nearly laughed with relief.
Then he asked, "Which application did I submit for this?"
"You were automatically selected."
"By whom? Can you email me from an official address?"
The caller grew impatient. "The offer expires in one hour."
"Then I'll call back," Hrithik said, and hung up.
He walked straight into the scholarship section. Alka Ma'am, who handled every award in the college, checked the official scholarship portal. "No such award. And no real scholarship asks you to pay to receive money."
"I didn't think so," Hrithik said. "Why would a stranger give me fifty thousand?"
That afternoon Alka Ma'am pinned a warning about the call on the notice board.

qa.a: He was standing in the corridor outside the college accounts office.

qa.q: What did Hrithik feel at first, and what changed?
qa.a: He felt a rush of relief at first, but his question about which application he submitted shows doubt taking over.

qa.q: Which of Hrithik's steps protected him best?
qa.a: Asking what he had entered, refusing to pay, and checking with Alka Ma'am on the official scholarship portal showed the award did not exist.

qa.q: How did Alka Ma'am use what Hrithik brought in?
qa.a: Alka Ma'am confirmed the scam and pinned a warning on the notice board, protecting other students from the same call.

grounding: A student asks what he entered, checks the claim through the official scholarship office, and refuses to pay a fee to receive a prize.

passage:
Hi Sachin,
You forwarded me that email about winning a car in the festival mega draw and asked if you should pay the 12,000 for registration and tax. Please don't. Here's what I did when I got almost the same one last month.
First, I asked myself one question: what did I enter? Nothing. Nobody hands a stranger a car.
Second, I didn't use any number or link in the email. I went to the company's official website myself and found their customer care. They said they run no such draw and asked me to forward it to their fraud team.
Third, I reminded myself that a genuine prize doesn't ask you to pay before you get it.
I also reported the email on the cybercrime portal. It took five minutes.
If you've already paid anything, call me tonight. We'll sort it out together, no lectures.
Lalit

qa.q: How much did the email ask Sachin to pay?
qa.a: It asked Sachin to pay 12,000 for registration and tax.

qa.q: What does Lalit's "no lectures" suggest about how Lalit feels towards Sachin?
qa.a: It suggests Lalit cares and wants Sachin to feel safe asking for help, without shame if money was already paid.

qa.q: Which of Lalit's steps would help Sachin most, and why?
qa.a: Going to the company's official website instead of using the email's links, because it checks the claim through a separate channel the scammer cannot control.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel reading the email?
qa.a: Sachin may feel disappointed that there is no car, but relieved to have clear steps and someone ready to help.

grounding: Lalit explains to Sachin how asking what was entered, checking the company's official site and refusing a fee exposed a fake prize.

Ayesha, you'll love this. So I'm Tarun, right, on my way to class, and I get a call. A man, very excited. "Sir, congratulations! You have won ₹25 lakh in our TV quiz lottery!"
For one second my heart did a little jump. Twenty-five lakh.
Then I asked, "Which quiz did I enter?" He said, "Your number was selected automatically." I said, "So I entered nothing." He laughed and said I just had to pay ₹10,000 "processing fee" and the money would come.
I said, "Why would a stranger give me lakhs and ask me to pay first? Deduct it from the prize." He got angry. Then he hung up.
I checked the channel's official website. There was a big red warning: "We never call winners asking for money."
A real prize doesn't need a fee first. I reported the number and posted the warning in our class group. Three people said they'd got the same call.

qa.a: ₹25 lakh.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel for a moment when he heard the amount?
qa.a: Tarun felt a quick jump of excitement, before becoming suspicious and asking questions.

qa.q: What did Tarun do that protected him?
qa.a: He asked what he had entered, refused to pay, checked the official website, reported the number and warned his class group.

qa.q: How did the caller react to Tarun's question?
qa.a: The caller got angry and hung up, because a real prize giver would not mind being asked to deduct the fee.

grounding: A young adult asks what he entered and why a stranger would give him money, checks official channels and refuses to pay for a prize.

I'm Bhupen, Jahnavi's older brother. I was sitting across the dining table when her phone rang on Sunday, so I heard her side of it.
"Won? Won what?" She put it on speaker. A cheerful woman said Jahnavi had won a laptop in a college lucky draw.
Jahnavi frowned. "Which college draw? What did I enter?"
"It was based on your student ID."
"Which company is running it?"
The woman named a company. Jahnavi typed it into her laptop while listening. "And the fee?"
"Just ₹2,000 for courier and GST, madam."
"You can take the courier charge from the prize value," Jahnavi said. The woman's voice changed and the call dropped.
Jahnavi called the college office's official number. They said there was no draw. She reported the number on the cybercrime portal.
I don't know what she was thinking, but she didn't look excited at any point. Just careful. I was impressed.

qa.a: Bhupen is impressed by how careful she was, though he can't be sure what she was thinking.

passage: Vasudha beti, you think these prize tricks started with phones? When I was twenty, working at the post office in Lucknow, a letter came for me on thick yellow paper. It said I had won a foreign lottery, a huge sum, and only had to send a "clearance fee" by money order. In those days that sum was a house. My friend Shafiq said, "Send it quick before they change their mind." But I kept asking myself one thing: what did I enter? I had never bought a foreign ticket in my life. Why would a stranger across the sea give money to Imran of Aminabad? So I took the letter to our postmaster, who wrote to the address it gave. The letter came back: no such company. Shafiq's cousin had sent his fee the month before. He never saw a paisa. A real prize never asks you to pay first, beti. Ask what you entered, and check with someone official.

qa.a: Taking the letter to the postmaster, who wrote to the address, checked the claim through an official channel before any money was sent.

qa.a: He sent his fee and never saw a paisa; he likely felt cheated and ashamed.
